title: MODULE 10 — Frontend Data Engineering, Forms and API Integration

overview.text: Module overview

Modern frontend applications do not operate independently. They continuously communicate with backend services, retrieve information, submit user actions, validate information, manage cached data, and synchronize the interface with changing server information.
Consider a learning platform such as PrepSpaces.
A student opens the course catalogue. The frontend needs to retrieve course information from an API, display the results, and provide search and filtering.
The student then enrolls in a course. The frontend submits the enrollment request, waits for the backend response, and updates the interface.
Later, the student uploads an assignment, edits their profile, and receives an updated notification.
All these operations require a reliable frontend data-management architecture.

Module 06 introduced browser APIs, asynchronous JavaScript, Fetch, and WebSockets. Module 07 introduced TypeScript and runtime validation. Module 08 introduced React components and forms. Module 09 introduced advanced React architecture and state management.
Module 10 combines those skills to build frontend applications that communicate reliably with backend systems.
Important architectural boundary
This module focuses exclusively on the frontend side of data integration.
Included in this module | Covered in Backend & API Engineering
Calling REST API endpoints | Designing and implementing API endpoints
Processing API responses | Backend business logic
Fetching and caching data | Database design and queries
Managing forms and validation | Server-side validation implementation
Sending authentication information | Authentication and authorization enforcement
Uploading files from the browser | File storage infrastructure
Displaying real-time updates | WebSocket server implementation
Handling errors returned by services | Backend exception handling
Managing client-side state | Server-side persistence and transactions
Students should learn how to integrate a backend capability safely without being required to build that backend capability again.
Frontend data integration architecture
React User Interface — Pages, components, search, forms and tables
Frontend Data Layer — Hooks, TanStack Query, form state and validation
API Integration Layer — Fetch, request configuration, authentication context and response processing
HTTP / WebSocket -> Backend Services (Existing external APIs and services — outside this module's implementation scope)
The frontend controls how information is retrieved, presented, validated, cached, and synchronized. The backend remains responsible for authoritative data and permissions.
What you will learn
By completing this module, students should be able to:
Understand frontend-backend communication architecture.
Integrate REST APIs into React applications.
Create reusable API service layers.
Manage loading, success, empty, and error states.
Fetch and synchronize server data with TanStack Query.
Differentiate server state from client state.
Implement caching, refetching, and cache invalidation.
Develop pagination, filtering, and search interfaces.
Implement optimistic updates and rollback strategies.
Develop maintainable forms and controlled inputs.
Validate form information using Zod.
Manage complex forms using React Hook Form.
Handle authentication state and frontend credential handling.
Upload files and display upload progress.
Integrate real-time updates using WebSockets.

REST APIs commonly use HTTP methods to interact with resources.
The frontend must send the correct method and request data.
It must also understand that a successful HTTP request does not necessarily mean every expected business operation occurred as intended. The application should interpret the actual response.
JSON is a common data format for communication between frontend and backend systems.

Remember that TypeScript interfaces do not validate the actual network response. The data must be checked at runtime when it comes from an external source.

However, production applications should normally retrieve dynamic information from backend services.

3.1 Why an API service layer is needed
Imagine every React component creates its own Fetch request.
This makes the application harder to maintain.
A reusable API service layer centralizes this logic.
Instead of every component managing raw HTTP requests, components call typed functions.

React Component

Custom Hook
       ↓
Feature API Service
       ↓
Shared HTTP Client
       ↓
Backend API
Each layer has a defined responsibility.
Custom Hook: Connects application state with data operations.
Feature API service: Defines course-specific operations.
HTTP client: Handles common request behaviour.
This client provides common request handling.

The credentials: "include" option is appropriate when the authentication architecture uses cookies that must be included in cross-origin requests, subject to browser cookie and CORS rules. It can be adapted to the chosen authentication mechanism.

3.5 Why API services should not contain UI logic
Avoid putting React-specific rendering logic into the service.
For example, this is a poor service design:
A service should perform its data operation and return the result or throw an error.
The component or custom Hook should decide how the interface responds.
A reusable service layer can define application-specific errors.
The HTTP client can then throw structured errors:

A more complete client should also handle empty responses such as HTTP 204, non-JSON responses, network failures, and cancellation.

sections.title: Managing Loading, Success, Empty and Error States

blocks.text: An API request does not immediately provide information.
Between sending a request and receiving its response, the frontend needs to communicate what is happening.
Consider a student opening their courses page.
The course information is still being retrieved.
The request succeeded, but the student has no enrolled courses.
These are four distinct application states.
A professional frontend should explicitly handle each one.
Loading — Request in progress: Display a skeleton or loading indicator.
Success — Data retrieved successfully: React Engineering 75% (Course information is available.)
Empty — No matching records: No courses found. Enroll in a course to get started.
Error — Request unsuccessful: Unable to load courses. Check your connection and try again.
A discriminated union is useful for representing these states.
This provides a reusable model for different API-driven pages.
CoursesSchema should be defined using the runtime validation approach from Module 07.
4.5 Understanding initial loading versus background fetching
Initial loading: The application has no usable data yet.
Background fetching: The application already has data but is requesting an updated version.
For example, the student is already viewing 10 courses, and the application is refreshing their information.
It is usually better to keep displaying existing information while the refresh occurs, rather than replacing the entire page with a full-screen loading indicator.
This distinction becomes easier to manage using TanStack Query.
When an API request fails, the frontend should provide an appropriate recovery action.
Avoid automatically retrying all errors. Authentication failures, invalid data, and many other errors require different handling from temporary network failures.
Practical exercise: Build a reusable ApiStateView component that supports loading skeletons, successful results, empty states, error messages, and retry actions.
5.1 Why ordinary Fetch is not enough for larger applications
In Module 06, you learned how to retrieve data using Fetch.
However, larger applications require more sophisticated data management.
Imagine an application with these pages:
Several components may request the same information.
Without a shared data-fetching system, developers may need to manually manage:
TanStack Query: A library for managing asynchronous server data, caching, refetching and synchronization in frontend applications.
TanStack Query was previously known as React Query.
It helps developers manage data obtained from APIs.
Its primary purpose is managing server state, rather than replacing every form of React state. (TanStack Query React Docs)
TanStack Query uses a QueryClient to manage its query cache and related configuration.
retry allows one retry for failed queries.
refetchOnWindowFocus enables background refetching when the window is focused and the query is stale.
These are example application preferences, not universal settings.
Now descendant components can use TanStack Query Hooks.
useQuery retrieves and manages asynchronous data.
queryKey — Uniquely identifies the requested data.
queryFn — The function that retrieves the data and returns a Promise.
This component no longer needs to manually manage multiple state variables for the common query lifecycle.
Query keys are central to TanStack Query.
Each key identifies a particular cached data request.
When courseId changes, the query key changes.
This allows TanStack Query to distinguish between different course records.
Any variable that affects the fetched result should generally be included in the query key.
Sometimes one request depends on information from another.
For example, a student's assignments should only be loaded after their student ID is available.
TanStack Query supports the enabled option.
The query is not automatically executed until the required condition is satisfied.
For a query that has no valid input yet, current versions also provide skipToken for type-safe query disabling.
Mutations commonly create, update, or delete information.
Once the backend confirms the creation, the course query is invalidated so that active course data can be refreshed.
Current TanStack Query documentation explains both queries and mutations as distinct tools for fetching and changing server data. (TanStack Query React Docs)
isPending | Query has no data and is pending
isFetching | A fetch operation is in progress
isError | Query is in an error state
The exact status behaviour should be understood alongside the installed TanStack Query version and its documentation.
Practical exercise: Connect a React course catalogue to TanStack Query. Implement course retrieval, detail queries, creation mutations, deletion mutations, and query invalidation.
Not all application data comes from the same place.
Course records retrieved from the backend.
These values have different owners and lifecycles.
Treating all of them as the same type of state can make an application harder to maintain.
Server state is information whose authoritative source is an external service or backend.
It may change outside the current browser.
TanStack Query is specifically designed to manage this category of information.
Client state represents information managed within the current frontend application.
These values do not necessarily require a backend request each time they change.
React state and Context are useful for managing them.
Authoritative owner | Backend service | Frontend application
Background refresh | Often needed | Usually unnecessary
Typical tools | TanStack Query | useState, useReducer, Context
Examples | Courses and assignments | Modal and selected tab
Suppose a course is retrieved using TanStack Query.
Then the developer copies it into a separate Context state:
Now the application maintains two copies of the same server information:
For example, TanStack Query may receive updated course information while Context still contains the old version.
Avoid duplicating server data into global React state without a clear reason.
Student profile from API | TanStack Query
Current login/session view | Auth Context or auth integration
A single application can use several state-management approaches together.
Do not move server data into client state just because multiple components need it.
TanStack Query already shares cached query data across components subscribing to the same query key.
Similarly, use Context for shared application information rather than duplicating all API information into a global provider.
Frontend updates or invalidates relevant queries.
Enrolled course and dashboard information become synchronized.
The frontend should not independently assume that an enrollment has become authoritative simply because the user clicked the button.

Practical exercise: Examine a React dashboard and classify every state variable as server state, client state, authentication-related state, or form state. Redesign the application so each piece of information has a clear owner.

Without an appropriate caching strategy, the application may repeatedly retrieve the same information.
Caching allows previously retrieved information to be reused.
TanStack Query maintains a client-side cache of query results.
Each query can have cached information.
When another component requests data using the same query key, it can use the existing cache instead of necessarily starting a new request.
staleTime determines how long cached data is considered fresh.
Here, the data is considered fresh for one minute after a successful fetch.
During this period, normal staleness-based refetching is not needed.
gcTime controls how long inactive cached query data remains available before being garbage-collected.
The two settings solve different problems:
gcTime | Determines retention of inactive cache data
A query can be stale while still being present in the cache.
A stale query being mounted again.
This requests updates at a 30-second interval while the query is eligible for refetching.
Periodic requests should be used thoughtfully, particularly for large dashboards or APIs with rate limits.
The official documentation explains how stale data is refreshed and how freshness can be configured using staleTime. (TanStack Query React Docs)
Suppose a user creates a new course.
The previously cached course list no longer represents the latest server information.
The frontend can invalidate the relevant query.
Invalidation marks matching queries as stale and can trigger refetching for active queries.
Sometimes the application already knows the exact information returned by a successful mutation.
Instead of waiting for a full refetch, developers can update the cache directly.
This can be appropriate when the server response is authoritative and the frontend knows which cached records need updating.
This helps create predictable query keys.
After a course is updated, developers may invalidate:
Or invalidate only specific query groups when broad invalidation would cause too much unnecessary fetching.

API request
     ↓
Successful response
     ↓
Data stored in cache
     ↓
Other components reuse cached data
     ↓
Data eventually becomes stale
     ↓
Refetch or invalidate
     ↓
Updated data replaces old data
Using the same query key for different data.
Excluding filter parameters from a query key.
Keeping rapidly changing data fresh for too long.
Refetching every endpoint on every user action.
Assuming stale cached data is always unusable.
Treating cached frontend data as an authoritative security source.
Practical exercise: Configure caching for courses, student profiles, and assignments. Experiment with staleTime, gcTime, window-focus refetching, direct cache updates, and query invalidation.
Imagine an application containing 50,000 courses or student records.
Displaying every record simultaneously can be inefficient.
Pagination divides a large dataset into smaller groups.
Client-side pagination takes an already retrieved collection and divides it into smaller groups.
This approach is suitable when the full dataset is already reasonably small and available in the browser.
For large datasets, the frontend generally requests only the records needed for the current page.
The backend returns only the requested page, together with pagination metadata.
The frontend displays the records and uses the metadata to control navigation.
The actual pagination calculation and data selection remain backend responsibilities.
A production component should also use the actual totalPages value to prevent navigating beyond the available records.
Search interfaces allow users to find information by entering text.
The component can pass the search value to the API.
When the search term changes, the page should normally reset to the first page.
Suppose users should filter courses by level:
The frontend can expose: All Levels, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced.
The backend filters the actual records, while the frontend controls the selection and displays results.
Users might need to sort courses by:
A sort option can be represented as:
The frontend includes the selected option in the request.
8.8 Integrating filtering and pagination with TanStack Query
Notice that the search, filter, and page values form part of the query key.
This ensures that different combinations of filters and pages have distinct cache entries.
TanStack Query provides keepPreviousData for pagination transitions through the placeholderData option.
This allows the previous results to remain visible while the next page is being fetched.
The interface can show a subtle loading indicator without clearing the entire list. (TanStack Query React Docs)
Without debouncing, a search field may generate one API request for every keystroke.
A debounced search value waits until the user stops typing.

const [search, setSearch] = useState("");
const debouncedSearch = useDebouncedValue(search, 300);
Use debouncedSearch in the query key and request.
8.11 What the frontend should not assume
The frontend should not independently decide that a filter result contains every available record if the backend supports server-side pagination.
It must respect the API's actual pagination contract.
Similarly, filtering only the currently loaded page does not produce a global filter over the complete server dataset.
Practical exercise: Build a course catalogue with server-side pagination, debounced search, sorting, filters, previous/next controls, and TanStack Query caching.
Consider a student completing a lesson.
The student clicks: Mark as completed
The frontend sends an update request to the backend.
A traditional implementation might wait for the backend response before changing the interface.
However, this can make the application feel slow.
For common interactions, the frontend can update the interface immediately and then synchronize with the backend.
This is called an optimistic update.
When the user completes another lesson, the interface can immediately display:
The request is still running in the background.
If the backend confirms the operation, the optimistic update becomes the confirmed state.
If the request fails, the frontend must restore or reconcile the previous state.
User performs an action — Completes a lesson
Success: Keep confirmed data and synchronize cache.
Failure: Rollback or refetch authoritative data.
9.4 Implementing optimistic updates with TanStack Query
TanStack Query supports optimistic updates through mutation lifecycle callbacks.
This example assumes that the application's Course type and completeLesson service match the mutation contract.
Roll back if the operation fails.
The official TanStack Query documentation describes this lifecycle using onMutate, onError, and onSettled. (TanStack Query React Docs)
Rollback means reverting a temporary optimistic change after the operation fails.
A student clicks a button to enroll.
But the server rejects the enrollment because the course is unavailable.
The frontend must restore the previous state: Enroll
The user should also see an appropriate explanation.
Optimistic updates are not appropriate for every operation.
The action is likely to succeed.
The interface benefits from immediate feedback.
Actions with uncertain server-side business rules.
Synchronization means keeping the frontend's displayed information aligned with the authoritative server information.
The frontend should never assume that its cached representation is always the latest authoritative information.
Practical exercise: Build an optimistic lesson-completion interface. Implement immediate progress updates, successful synchronization, failed-request rollback, and an error message.
Forms are among the most important parts of a frontend application.
Consider a course management application with several forms:
A small form may contain only two fields.
A production form can contain dozens of fields, multiple validation rules, conditional fields, and complex user interactions.
Without a proper architecture, forms can become difficult to manage.

User enters information

Input values are collected

A controlled input receives its value from React state.
The React state is the source of truth for the input's displayed value.
Now the same input structure can be reused across the application.
A controlled implementation stores these values in React state.
Input updates | React handlers | Browser input behaviour
Validation | Easy to integrate | Uses DOM values or form libraries
Data access | State | Refs or form APIs
Common use | Custom form interfaces | Large and integration-oriented forms
For large forms, libraries such as React Hook Form help reduce unnecessary state management and simplify validation.
Prevent the browser's default page navigation when appropriate.
Preserve user input appropriately after failure.
A successful user interface should not clear the form just because the submit button was clicked. Wait for the operation to succeed.
This associates the label with the correct control.
Practical exercise: Create a reusable course form that supports create and edit operations, controlled inputs, submission feedback, accessibility, and validation.
These values are not appropriate for the application.
The frontend should identify invalid information before sending it to the backend.
Zod provides a schema-based validation approach.
Zod: A TypeScript-oriented library for validating runtime data and deriving static types.
Zod can validate information at runtime.
Zod also allows developers to infer TypeScript types from validation schemas. (Zod)
A title of at least three characters.
A maximum title length of 100 characters.
A minimum description length of ten characters.
Instead of manually defining a separate TypeScript interface:
Now the TypeScript type is derived from the schema.
This prevents the static definition and runtime validation rules from unnecessarily diverging.
The parse() method validates a value.
If the data is invalid, it throws a ZodError.
This is useful when the application wants validation failures to enter an exception-handling flow.
For form validation, safeParse() is often convenient.
The returned result is a discriminated union.
It contains either validated data or validation issues.
Only validated data is passed to the frontend API service.
Remember that the backend must perform its own validation.
Frontend validation can be bypassed by anyone sending direct requests to the API.
Now the schema checks the relationship between two fields.
Sometimes form inputs and API data have different types.
For example, HTML number inputs usually provide string values.
This attempts to convert compatible input values into numbers before validation.
Be careful with coercion: values such as an empty string can have surprising numeric conversions. Define explicit checks when empty values are not permitted.
Checks source-code type usage | Checks actual runtime values
Works during development and compilation | Works while the application executes
Defines expected structures | Validates received information
Types disappear from ordinary JS output | Performs real validation
Practical exercise: Create Zod schemas for Student Registration, Course Creation, Assignment Submission, and Profile Editing. Add required-field, range, format, and cross-field validation.

sections.title: Advanced Form Management with React Hook Form

blocks.text: 12.1 Why React Hook Form is needed
A simple registration form can be managed with useState.
However, consider a course creation form containing:
Now imagine an administrative form containing 30 or more fields.
Managing every input with separate React state can become difficult.
React Hook Form provides a specialized form-management system.
React Hook Form: A React library for managing form values, registration, validation, errors, and submissions.
It uses uncontrolled native inputs by default, which can reduce the need for React re-renders on every keystroke. It also supports controlled components through Controller.
The React Hook Form documentation provides TypeScript support and resolver integration for external validation libraries. (React Hook Form)
register() connects an input to React Hook Form.
The register function supplies the properties and event handlers needed for the form library to track that input.
It also establishes the input's field name.
It generally performs the configured validation before calling the successful submission callback.
If validation fails, the invalid form data is not passed to that callback.
12.7 Integrating React Hook Form with Zod
The Zod resolver converts the schema's validation result into React Hook Form's error structure.
defaultValues define the initial values of a form.
This is especially useful when editing existing information.
For example, an existing course can be loaded and the form can be initialized with its current values.
React Hook Form also provides reset() for updating form values after a record has been retrieved.
React Hook Form provides useful information about the current form.
isDirty | Whether values have changed from their defaults
isSubmitting | Whether submission is in progress
isValid | Whether the current form is valid according to its configured mode
touchedFields | Fields that have been touched
dirtyFields | Fields whose values differ from their defaults
isSubmitSuccessful | Whether the most recent submission completed successfully
These values help build professional form interfaces.
Some inputs are not native HTML elements.
React Hook Form provides Controller for connecting controlled components.
Controller provides the field properties needed to integrate the component with the form.
When an API operation fails, the form should remain recoverable.
Do not clear the user's entered information after an unsuccessful request unless the interaction specifically requires it.
12.12 When should you use React Hook Form?
For a simple two-field input, ordinary React state can be perfectly sufficient.
Practical exercise: Build a complete course creation and editing form using React Hook Form, Zod, TypeScript, nested fields, default values, validation feedback, and API submission handling.

sections.title: Authentication State and Token Handling in Frontend Applications

blocks.text: A frontend application often needs to know whether a user is authenticated.
The frontend must manage the user-facing parts of this process.
However, the backend is responsible for actually verifying credentials, issuing or validating sessions, and enforcing permissions.
Authentication answers: Who is the user?
Authorization answers: What is this user allowed to access or perform?
Student | Successfully signed in | Access permitted student resources
Instructor | Successfully signed in | Access permitted instructor features
Administrator | Successfully signed in | Access permitted administrative operations
Guest | Not authenticated | Only public functionality
The frontend can use the current session information to display appropriate navigation and interfaces.
It cannot independently grant permission to backend operations.

User submits login form
         ↓
Frontend sends login request
         ↓
Backend verifies credentials
         ↓
Authentication result returned
         ↓
Frontend updates session-aware UI
         ↓
Protected pages become accessible
         ↓
Authenticated API requests continue
The exact credential and session mechanism depends on the backend's authentication architecture.
A frontend might maintain a typed session model:
This allows the UI to represent:
Depending on the architecture, the browser may use:
A common approach is a server-managed session cookie configured with suitable security attributes, including:
The HttpOnly attribute prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie through document.cookie.
The browser can still include an eligible cookie in requests.
13.6 Why LocalStorage is risky for authentication credentials
One major security mistake is storing sensitive authentication credentials in LocalStorage.
This makes the credential available to JavaScript running on the same origin.
If an XSS vulnerability exists, malicious JavaScript may be able to read it.

OWASP recommends against storing session identifiers, access tokens, refresh tokens, and other authentication credentials in LocalStorage or SessionStorage. It discusses secure HttpOnly cookies and BFF architectures as alternatives. (OWASP Cheat Sheet Series)
This does not mean LocalStorage has no use. It can be suitable for non-sensitive preferences and other appropriate client-side information.
For a same-origin application, the browser normally includes eligible cookies according to cookie rules.
For a cross-origin request where the authentication architecture requires cookies:
This requires appropriate server-side CORS and cookie configuration.
The frontend cannot force the browser to send a cookie that violates its security attributes or browser policies.
Some APIs use bearer access tokens.
The frontend adds the token to the Authorization header:
The token must come from the application's approved authentication flow.
Do not place privileged server credentials in frontend code.
If a token must be held in browser memory, developers need an appropriate lifecycle and threat model. Avoid treating LocalStorage as a safe default.
Consider a student who leaves the platform open for several hours.
The next API request could return: 401 Unauthorized
Attempt the authentication provider's approved renewal mechanism, if applicable.
Redirect to login when the session cannot be recovered.
A shared API client can centralize common request handling.
However, it should not attempt to implement server authentication or invent its own security protocol.
The frontend can use the role information from the authenticated session to present different navigation.
Hiding an administrator link improves the user experience, but it does not secure the endpoint.
The backend must independently enforce authorization for every protected operation.

Practical exercise: Integrate an existing authentication service into a React application. Implement session initialization, authentication-aware navigation, login and logout interfaces, expired-session handling, and authenticated API requests. Do not implement the authentication backend.
Many frontend applications allow users to submit files.
The frontend needs to allow users to select files, validate them, submit them, and communicate upload status.
When a user selects a file through an HTML file input, JavaScript can access it through the File API.
type | MIME type provided by the browser
The MIME type and filename are useful for client-side feedback but must not be trusted as security verification.
However, actual file verification, content scanning, and size enforcement must happen through the receiving service.
The browser can create a temporary URL for a selected File object.
The object URL is released when the selected file changes or the component is cleaned up.
The browser provides FormData for sending form fields and files in multipart requests.
Do not manually set the Content-Type: multipart/form-data header when sending FormData through Fetch or XMLHttpRequest.
The browser must generate the multipart boundary and include it in the header.
Users should know whether their file is still uploading.
For example: Uploading resume.pdf — 75% — Please do not close the page.
However, there is an important technical distinction.
The Fetch API does not provide the same straightforward upload-progress event interface as XMLHttpRequest.
When upload progress is required, XMLHttpRequest.upload can be used.
The receiving endpoint and returned JSON must match the application's actual API contract.
The XMLHttpRequest.upload interface supports progress events, allowing the frontend to calculate the transfer percentage. (MDN)
A production frontend should account for:
Large applications may use direct-to-storage upload URLs or multipart upload services, but the storage workflow and authorization rules belong to the backend or storage infrastructure.
Practical exercise: Build a course thumbnail uploader with file selection, frontend validation, image preview, progress tracking, cancellation, and upload-result handling.

sections.title: Real-Time Data Integration and WebSocket Interfaces

blocks.text: Traditional API integration often follows a request-response pattern.
The student opens the notification page.
The backend returns the current notifications.
But what happens when a new notification arrives while the student is already viewing the dashboard?
Without a real-time communication mechanism, the frontend may not know about the new information until it requests the data again.
Applications that need timely updates benefit from real-time communication.
WebSocket API: A browser API for persistent, bidirectional communication between a client and a server.
Unlike ordinary HTTP request-response communication, WebSockets allow both endpoints to send messages through an established connection.
The browser can receive new information without repeatedly polling an API.

Frontend <--- Response ---- Backend

Phase 1 — Application foundation: Set up React, TypeScript, Vite, routing, shared components, and API configuration.
Phase 2 — REST API services: Implement reusable HTTP requests, typed API functions, and runtime response validation.
Phase 3 — Data fetching: Integrate TanStack Query, query keys, loading states, caching, and refetching.
Phase 4 — Course catalogue: Implement course listing, search, sorting, filtering, and server-side pagination.
Phase 5 — Course forms: Integrate React Hook Form, Zod, creation forms, editing forms, and validation feedback.
Phase 6 — Mutations and synchronization: Implement course creation, updates, deletion, cache invalidation, and optimistic updates.
Phase 7 — Authentication integration: Connect the existing authentication service and implement session-aware API requests.
Phase 8 — File uploads: Implement file selection, validation, previews, upload progress, and error handling.
Phase 9 — Real-time integration: Integrate a supplied WebSocket service and synchronize relevant interface data.
Phase 10 — Testing and completion: Verify API behaviour, form validation, caching, authentication states, upload handling, and responsiveness.
